steps.working: Check the shapes: $A$ is $2 \times 2$ and $B$ is $2 \times 2$, so the inner numbers match and the answer is $2 \times 2$.
steps.decision: Two seconds of checking tells you the product exists and how many entries to produce. It also stops you starting a product that cannot be done. No mark is going for it; it protects the ones below.
Work along the row and down the column at the same time, and write the sum out before evaluating it. Sign slips live in this line.

options: Because the entry in row 1, column 1 comes from row 1 of the first and column 1 of the second
Because the entries in the same position are multiplied together
Because the first row of each matrix is multiplied term by term
whyMenu.explain: The position of the entry names the row to take from the first matrix and the column to take from the second.

steps.decision: Same row, next column. Keeping the row fixed while the column moves is what stops entries landing in the wrong place.

steps.working: Row 2 against column 1: $(2)(5) + (4)(-1) = 6$. Row 2 against column 2: $(2)(2) + (4)(0) = 4$.
steps.decision: Move to the second row and repeat. Four entries, four sums, in the same order every time. The second method mark is for all four being attempted, so it lands here.
Check the shape against step 1: four entries in a $2 \times 2$ matrix, which is what the shape rule promised.

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new method, so answer from what you already know.
What is $(2) \times (5) + (4) \times (-1)$?

options.feedback: $10$ and $-4$ add to $6$.
The second product is negative, because one of its two numbers is negative.
Only the first product has been used. Both products are added together.

items.stem: A rectangle of numbers has 2 rows and 3 columns. Which description is right?
items.skill: Reading a shape as rows by columns

options.feedback: Two rows of three, so six numbers. That count is worth doing before you start writing an answer.
The rows and columns are multiplied, not added.
Each of the two rows holds three numbers.

items.skill: Multiplying a negative by a positive

options.feedback: A negative multiplied by a positive stays negative.
The sign has been dropped. Three lots of a negative number is negative.
That is $3$ added rather than multiplied.

items.stem: Which of these is $A + B$, for $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$?

options.feedback: Each entry added to the entry in the same position.
The entries have been multiplied rather than added.
That is $B - A$. The question asked for the sum.

items.stem: Which of these is $AB$, for $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$?

options.feedback: Each entry is a row of $A$ paired with a column of $B$.
The entries in matching positions have been multiplied. A product pairs a whole row with a whole column.
Rows have been paired with rows. It is a row of the first against a column of the second.
That is $BA$. The order of a matrix product changes the answer.

items.stem: A matrix $P$ is $2 \times 2$ and a matrix $Q$ is $2 \times 3$. Which products exist?

options.feedback: For $PQ$ the inner numbers are $2$ and $2$, so it exists and comes out $2 \times 3$. For $QP$ they are $3$ and $2$, which do not match.
$QP$ has inner numbers $3$ and $2$. They do not match, so that product does not exist.

options.text: Neither, because the shapes are different
options.feedback: Multiplication does not need identical shapes. It needs the inner two numbers to match, and for $PQ$ they do.

items.stem: For a matrix $M$, what does $M^{2}$ mean?

options.feedback: A power is a repeated product, and matrix products are row by column.
That is the slip the reports name most often here. It gives a different matrix entirely.
Doubling is $2M$. Squaring is multiplying the matrix by itself.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows $A$, which is $2 \times 2$, and $C$, which is $2 \times 3$.
Identify the correct statement about $A + C$.

options.text: It does not exist, because the two matrices are different shapes
options.feedback: Adding pairs entries in matching positions, and $C$ has a third column with nothing opposite it.

options.text: It is a $2 \times 3$ matrix, with the extra column of $C$ copied across
options.feedback: Nothing is copied across in an addition. With no entry of $A$ opposite that third column, the sum does not exist.

options.text: It is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, using the first two columns of $C$
options.feedback: A matrix cannot be trimmed to fit. Addition needs the two shapes to be identical.

scheme.for: it does not exist: the shapes differ

hints: Compare the two shapes before anything else.
parts.workedSolution:
$A$ is $2 \times 2$ and $C$ is $2 \times 3$.
Addition pairs entries in matching positions, so it needs identical shapes. $A + C$ does not exist.

questions.solutionProgram: main: $A$ is $2 \times 2$ and $C$ is $2 \times 3$. Addition pairs entries in matching positions, so it needs identical shapes. $A + C$ does not exist.

parts.stem:
The matrices $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$.
Work out $AB$.
Write the answer as a matrix.

scheme.for: at least one entry from a row of $A$ against a column of $B$
all four entries attempted row by column

hints: Row 1 of $A$ with column 1 of $B$ gives the entry in row 1, column 1.
Work along the row and down the column, then add.
parts.workedSolution:
Row by column: $\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}16 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
For example row 2, column 1 is $(2)(5) + (4)(-1) = 6$.

commonErrors.feedback: The entries in matching positions have been multiplied. Each entry of a product is a whole row against a whole column, which gives $\begin{pmatrix}16 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
Rows of $A$ have been paired with rows of $B$. It is a row of the first against a column of the second, which gives $\begin{pmatrix}16 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
That is $BA$. The order of a matrix product changes the answer, and $AB$ is $\begin{pmatrix}16 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.

options.feedback: $A^{2}$ means $A \times A$, worked row by column.
Each entry has been squared. Squaring a matrix means multiplying it by itself, which gives $\begin{pmatrix}7 & -7 \\ 14 & 14\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows the matrices $A$, $B$ and $C$.
Work out $2A - B$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: Double every entry of $A$ first, then subtract position by position.

commonErrors.feedback: The subtraction is the wrong way round: that is $B - 2A$. Every entry changes sign, and $2A - B$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1 & -4 \\ 5 & 8\end{pmatrix}$.

Write the answer as a matrix.

hints: The shapes are $2 \times 2$ and $2 \times 3$, so the answer has six entries.

parts.stem: Explain why the product $CA$ cannot be worked out.

accepted: C has 3 columns and A has 2 rows, and they are not equal, so the product does not exist
the number of columns of C is 3 and the number of rows of A is 2, so they do not match

scheme.for: the columns of $C$ and the rows of $A$ do not match

hints: Write the two shapes side by side, $C$ first.
parts.workedSolution:
$C$ is $2 \times 3$ and $A$ is $2 \times 2$, so the product $CA$ has inner numbers $3$ and $2$.
C has 3 columns and A has 2 rows, and they are not equal, so the product does not exist.

questions.solutionProgram: a: $2A = \begin{pmatrix}6 & -2 \\ 4 & 8\end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting position by position: $2A - B = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -4 \\ 5 & 8\end{pmatrix}$. || b: $AC = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & 5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 12 & -11 \\ 14 & 8 & 16\end{pmatrix}$. For example row 2, column 3 is $(2)(-2) + (4)(5) = 16$. || c: $C$ is $2 \times 3$ and $A$ is $2 \times 2$, so the product $CA$ has inner numbers $3$ and $2$. C has 3 columns and A has 2 rows, and they are not equal, so the product does not exist.

findTheMistake.stem: Seán was asked to work out $AB$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. His working:
studentWorking: A is 2 x 2 and B is 2 x 2, so AB is 2 x 2
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 1 is right, and the shape he predicted is the shape he produced, so nothing looks wrong on the page.
Line 2 multiplies the two entries sitting in the same position. A matrix product pairs a whole row of the first with a whole column of the second, so that entry is $(3)(5) + (-1)(-1) = 16$.
Every line after it repeats the same pairing, so the whole matrix is wrong even though the arithmetic in each line is right.
findTheMistake.feedback: The shape you predicted is right and the arithmetic is accurate, so this is a method problem rather than a careless one. Each entry of a product is a sum of two products, never a single one: if a line of your working has no plus sign in it, you have paired the wrong things. Say "row of the first, column of the second" as you write each line.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the entry in row 2, column 1 of a matrix product?
prompts.answer: Take row 2 of the first matrix and column 1 of the second, multiply them term by term and add the results.

prompts.prompt: When can two matrices be added, and when can they be multiplied?
prompts.answer: Added only when they are the same shape. Multiplied only when the columns of the first match the rows of the second.

prompts.prompt: A matrix that is $m \times n$ is multiplied by one that is $n \times p$. What shape is the answer?
prompts.answer: It is $m \times p$: the inner numbers match, and the outer two give the shape of the product.

prompts.prompt: What does $M^{2}$ mean for a matrix $M$, and what does it not mean?
prompts.answer: It means $M \times M$, worked row by column. It does not mean squaring each entry.
No. Matrix multiplication depends on the order, and often only one of the two products exists at all.

prompts.prompt: What is the first thing to write down before multiplying two matrices?
prompts.answer: The two shapes, side by side. They say whether the product exists and how many entries the answer needs.
